source.name: Street Design Manual, 3rd edition: Glossary (NYC DOT)

terms.term: AASHTO (American Association of State Highway Transportation Officials)
terms.def: A nonprofit, nonpartisan association representing highway and transportation departments in the fifty states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, across air, highways, public transportation, rail and water. It publishes design guidance including A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets (the "Green Book").
The design of facilities and public right-of-way that are easy, safe and intuitive to use for people with disabilities. Accessible environments let a person navigate the space independently.

The federal law giving civil rights protections to people with disabilities, similar to protections based on race, color, sex, national origin, age and religion. It guarantees equal opportunity in public accommodations, employment, transportation, state and local government services, and telecommunications.
The average number of vehicles passing a point or using a roadway per day: total traffic volume over a period (in whole days) divided by the number of days. Sometimes called VPD (Vehicles Per Day).

A device that communicates pedestrian signal timing in non-visual formats such as audible tones, speech messages or vibrating surfaces. Installation in NYC is governed by the Accessible Pedestrian Signals Policy enacted October 21, 2019.
The part of the roadway system serving as the principal network for through-traffic, connecting areas of major traffic generation and important highways entering the city.
The elevation of surface water from a flood that has a 1% or higher annual chance of occurring in any given year.

Every two- or three-wheeled device a person rides, propelled by human power through a belt, chain or gears, with wheels in tandem or tricycle form. It excludes devices with solid tires meant only for sidewalk use by pre-teenage children. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 102; RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
A designated space marked with crosshatch or chevron markings that separates a bicycle facility from traffic and/or parking.

A general term for improvements and provisions made by public agencies to accommodate or encourage bicycling, including parking and storage facilities and shared roadways not specifically designated for bicycle use.

A dedicated on-street or grade-separated lane for bikes, typically delineated with markings, a curb or a parking lane within the roadway, or physically separated from the roadway for most of its length.

A bikeway designated by the jurisdiction with directional and informational route markers, with or without route numbers. In NYC the Street Design Manual sets out five types: Shared Lanes, Conventional Bike Lanes, One-Way Protected Bike Lanes, Two-Way Protected Bike Lanes, and Grade-Separated Bike Lanes.

A not-for-profit corporation of property owners and commercial tenants that promotes business development and quality of life. BIDs provide supplemental services such as sanitation, maintenance, public safety, visitor services, marketing, capital improvements and beautification, funded by a special assessment paid by property owners in the district.
A generic term for any road, street, path or way specifically designated in some manner for bicycle travel, whether exclusive to bicycles or shared with other modes.
A planted area, generally in the sidewalk, designed to collect and manage stormwater (rainwater) that runs off streets.

A short vertical post or similar structure that defines areas in the streetscape, often used to separate pedestrians or streetscape elements from vehicles. In a line, bollards keep motor vehicles out of pedestrian space such as sidewalks or plazas.

A flexible, high-performance rapid transit mode combining physical, operating and system elements into a permanent integrated system with a distinct identity, designed to improve the speed, reliability and attractiveness of bus service. Select Bus Service is NYC's application of BRT.
A vertical partition that prevents earth and fill from slipping into adjacent bodies of water.

Every motor vehicle seating more than fifteen adults plus the operator and used to transport people, and every charter, interstate, intrastate, school and sightseeing bus regardless of seating capacity. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
A street that carries one or more regularly scheduled local, commuter or intercity bus lines running on a published schedule.

A rating system, developed by the Illuminating Engineering Society (IES), describing the types of stray light escaping from an outdoor lighting fixture, making it easier to compare and evaluate outdoor luminaires.

Under City Charter Section 210, a project to construct, reconstruct, acquire or install a physical public improvement classified as a capital asset (including preliminary studies and financing costs), acquisition of permanent property, initial furnishings or equipment, improvements to streets, parks, bridges, tunnels, sewers and similar infrastructure, or other projects the local finance law allows with mayoral and comptroller approval.
A paving material, such as concrete, that is poured into place on site and set to harden.

The process by which City agencies review proposed discretionary actions to identify their environmental effects. It is NYC's way of implementing SEQR, the state law requiring government agencies to assess environmental effects before undertaking, funding or approving discretionary actions, unless exempt.
Separating or regulating conflicting traffic movements into definite paths using traffic islands or pavement markings, so vehicles and pedestrians move in an orderly way.
A straight, unobstructed path for pedestrian circulation on the sidewalk (RCNY Title 34, Section 7-06(c)(3)). DCWP's rules and the ADA also define clear path.

A detailed, project-specific analysis including a vulnerability and risk assessment, often followed by cost-benefit analysis, used to select investments in climate risk mitigation. Risk is assessed as a function of the likelihood and consequence of a given climate hazard.

A value between 0 and 1 measuring how slippery a surface is: the ratio of the resisting force on horizontal motion to the force pressing an object onto the surface. Lower values (like ice) are more slippery; higher values (like concrete) are less slippery.

A street that provides both land access and traffic circulation within residential, commercial and industrial areas, distributing trips from arterials into neighborhoods and channeling traffic from local streets into the arterial system. In the central business district the street grid may serve as the collector system.
A zoning district designated by the letter C (for example C1-2, C3, C4-7) where commercial uses are allowed and residential uses may also be permitted, as described in the Zoning Resolution.

In the Street Design Manual, streetscape elements that serve street users beyond infrastructure and vehicle operations, such as bike racks, newsstands, public and café seating, public art and plantings. They are generally authorized through permits, revocable consents and/or maintenance agreements. (Different from the zoning meaning.)

A grant by a City agency for private use of city-owned property in return for compensation beyond an administrative fee. Franchises, revocable consents and leases are not concessions. (NYC Charter Section 362(a))
The area created by extending the building line to the curb. (Mayor's Executive Order No. 22, April 13, 1995)
The corner plus 10 additional feet extending away from the intersection along each intersecting roadway.
A collision, as between two automobiles.

(A) The part of a roadway at an intersection within the extensions of the sidewalk lines on opposite sides, between the curbs or traversable roadway edges; or (B) any part of a roadway, at an intersection or elsewhere, marked for pedestrian crossing by lines or other surface markings. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 110)
Traffic using minor roadways, usually residential streets, as shortcuts to avoid congestion on major streets.
A vertical or sloping edge along a roadway that clearly defines the pavement edge. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 111)

A discharge of excess wastewater from a combined sewer system (one pipe carrying rainwater runoff, domestic sewage and industrial wastewater) directly into nearby waterways during heavy rain or snowmelt when volume exceeds the capacity of the sewer system or treatment plant.
The life expectancy of an asset or product as determined during design.

A selected speed used to determine a roadway's geometric design features. It should be logical given topography, anticipated operating speed, adjacent land use and the road's functional classification.
A selected vehicle, with representative weight, dimensions and operating characteristics, used to set roadway design controls for accommodating vehicles of designated classes.
Every person who operates, drives or is in actual physical control of a vehicle. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 113)
Every entrance or exit authorized under applicable law and used by vehicles to or from lands or buildings abutting a highway. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
A soil designed to achieve specific infiltration standards in a stormwater-capture installation.
A flat slab of stone used as a paving material.
A fixed vertical structure designed to prevent flooding from an adjacent river or waterway.

A grant by a City agency of a right to occupy or use the city's inalienable property (usually streets or sidewalks) to provide a public service. (NYC Charter Section 362(b)) Example: the Coordinated Street Furniture Franchise for bus shelters, newsstands, public toilets and bike shelters.

The section of sidewalk between the curb and the through (walking) zone where street furniture and amenities go, such as lighting, benches, wayfinding signs, utility poles, tree pits and bike parking. It may include green infrastructure like rain gardens. The Manual treats the street furniture/curb zone as the same thing.
A combination of traffic calming and visual measures at the entrance to a low-speed street to slow entering vehicles and discourage through-traffic.

Products, technologies and practices that use natural systems, or engineered systems that mimic them, to improve environmental quality and provide utility services. Typically soils and vegetation infiltrate, evapotranspire and/or detain stormwater; they can also filter air, reduce energy use, cool urban heat islands and store carbon.

A vegetated area and its pathways within the right-of-way under DOT jurisdiction and maintained by Parks under an agreement between the two agencies. Greenstreets do not include Stormwater Greenstreets.
Making infrastructure less susceptible to damage from external security, safety and climate threats, such as extreme wind, flooding or flying debris.
The entire width between the boundary lines of every publicly maintained way when any part is open to the public for vehicle travel. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 118)

The highest level of groundwater in an area, accounting for seasonal and storm-driven fluctuations. It varies across the boroughs and must be considered when designing stormwater management or green infrastructure.

An area that has a special character or special historical or aesthetic interest, represents one or more periods or styles of architecture typical of eras in the city's history, forms a distinct section of the city, and has been designated a historic district under Title 25 of the NYC Administrative Code (Section 25-302(h)).
Sideways movement of vehicles forced by physical and/or visual changes to roadway alignment, such as a bend in the road. A traffic calming technique.

terms.term: IESNA (Illuminating Engineering Society of North America)
terms.def: A professional organization of lighting engineers that has set recommended illumination levels for street and pedestrian lighting.
The process of creating convenient, safe and accessible spaces for everyone, with accessibility a critical component. The Manual uses "inclusive design" instead of "universal design."
The area within the grid created by extending the curblines of two or more streets where they cross. (RCNY Title 34, Section 2-01)

A light source that converts electricity to light through the movement of electrons, with no filament. It is more efficient than incandescent bulbs, uses less energy, is more compact and lasts longer.
A legally mapped street temporarily closed to motor vehicles by DOT, in accordance with authorized signs or other traffic control devices. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-12(r)(4))
A street not on the higher (collector or arterial) systems. It mainly provides direct access to abutting land and to higher-order streets; through-traffic is usually discouraged.
Vehicle traffic whose trip origin and/or destination is in the immediate area of a given street.

A method of measuring traffic flow based on delay and congestion, defined in the Highway Capacity Manual, graded A (free flow) to F (traffic jam). Historically used mainly for motor vehicles, LOS methods also exist for pedestrians, cyclists and transit.

Every vehicle operated or driven on a public highway that is propelled by any power other than muscular power, except as provided in Section 125 of the Vehicle and Traffic Law. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))

terms.term: MUTCD (Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices)
terms.def: The national standard, incorporated in federal regulations (23 CFR Part 655, Subpart F), for all traffic control devices (signs, signals, markings and other devices that regulate, warn or guide traffic) on any street, highway, bikeway, walkway, parking facility or private road open to public travel.

terms.term: NACTO (National Association of City Transportation Officials)
terms.def: A 501(c)(3) nonprofit that represents large cities on transportation issues and shares ideas, data and best practices. It publishes design guidance including the Urban Street Design Guide.
The speed drivers are observed traveling in free-flow conditions. The 85th percentile of observed speeds is the most common measure.
The standing of a vehicle, occupied or not, other than temporarily while actually loading or unloading property or passengers. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))

The hour or hours of greatest vehicle traffic volume on a street or intersection, usually defined for weekday AM, mid-day and PM, and Saturday mid-day peak periods. Traffic analyses typically study peak hours rather than a whole day.

A bicycle with fully operable pedals and an electric motor under 750 watts (one horsepower) that engages only while the rider pedals and the bike is under 20 miles per hour, and cuts out when the rider brakes, stops pedaling or reaches 20 mph. It may not have a throttle or other added motorized equipment. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))

An area designated by DOT for pedestrian circulation, use and enjoyment on property under DOT jurisdiction, such as a mapped public place or the bed of a roadway. It may include tables, seating, trees, plants, lighting, bike racks or public art. (NYC Administrative Code Section 19-157)

terms.term: A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets
terms.def: An AASHTO publication, often called the "Green Book," containing design practices in universal use as the standard for highway geometric design.
Any highway, road, street, avenue, alley, public place, public driveway or other public way. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 134)
Any person on foot or in a wheelchair. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 130)
A planted depression that captures and absorbs rainwater that would otherwise flow into a storm drain, mainly through infiltration and evapotranspiration.

The ability of people, places and infrastructure (such as transportation and energy) to withstand a stress or shock, recover and emerge stronger. In the Manual it refers to climate threats: sea-level rise, coastal storms, extreme precipitation and heat.
A legally mapped street permanently closed to motor vehicles by DOT and open to pedestrians. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-12(r)(4))

A grant by the City, revocable at will, to a property owner (or, with the owner's consent, a tenant) to use adjacent inalienable City property, usually streets or sidewalks, for purposes permitted by DOT or DoITT rules. (NYC Charter Section 362(c)(2); RCNY Title 34, Section 7-01)
A general term for land, property or interest in it, usually a strip, acquired for or devoted to transportation.
An open way on land for the passage of vehicles, people or animals.
The graded portion of a highway within its top and side slopes, prepared as a foundation for the pavement and shoulder.
The portion of a street designed, improved or ordinarily used for vehicle travel, not including the shoulder and slope. (RCNY Title 34, Section 2-01)

New York City's version of Bus Rapid Transit, connecting neighborhoods with limited transit options to subway stations and major destinations. Tools include off-board fare payment, bus lanes, Transit Signal Priority and longer spacing between stops.

Marking concrete's surface for visual or texture effect. "Tooled joint" scoring finishes sidewalk flag joints with a hand-troweled border; "simulated saw-cut joint" scoring uses a spacer to mimic joints cut with a masonry saw.

A bikeway physically separated from motor vehicle traffic by open space or a barrier, within a highway right-of-way or its own right-of-way. Pedestrians, skaters, wheelchair users, joggers and other non-motorized users may also use it.

The portion of a street, paved or unpaved, between the curb or roadway edge and adjacent property lines, intended for pedestrians. Where unclear, it is the area between the building line and the curb. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
An action to prevent pollution where it originates.
Stopping and/or reducing pollutants at their point of generation so they do not come into contact with stormwater.
Stopping a vehicle, occupied or not, other than temporarily while actually receiving or discharging passengers. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 145; RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Any halting of a vehicle, even momentarily, whether occupied or not. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
The abnormal rise of water generated by a storm, over and above the predicted astronomical tides.

A street, avenue, road, alley, lane, highway, boulevard, concourse, parkway, driveway, culvert, sidewalk, crosswalk, boardwalk and viaduct, and every class of public road, square and place, except marginal streets. (NYC Charter Section 210.7)
A tree growing in the public right-of-way. Street trees provide benefits ranging from higher property values to stormwater capture and urban heat island relief.
Industrial by-products used in concrete that would otherwise go to landfills, saving manufacturers money and reducing environmental impact.

The speed vehicles should travel on a street given the level of walking, biking and other activity generated by adjacent land uses, balancing vehicle mobility with safety for pedestrians and cyclists. It is usually the posted speed limit.
A network of devices deployed on surfaces to reduce flood impacts to buildings, roadways and other assets.
Vehicle traffic whose trip origin and destination are not in the immediate area of a given street.
Pedestrians, ridden or herded animals, vehicles, bicycles and other conveyances, singly or together, using any highway for travel. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 152)

Speed management that supports the livability of residential and commercial areas by improving safety, mobility and comfort for non-motorists, usually by reducing vehicle speeds or volumes. Measures include horizontal, vertical, lane narrowing and roadside interventions and other self-enforcing physical or perceptual features.
All signs, signals, markings and devices placed by a public body or official with jurisdiction to regulate, warn or guide traffic. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 153)

Except as otherwise specified in RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b), any vehicle or combination of vehicles designed to transport property that has either two axles and six tires, or three or more axles. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-13(a))
A paving material that is precast (such as a hexagonal asphalt paver) or individually cut (such as a granite block), so each piece can be removed or replaced individually.

Every device in, upon or by which a person or property is or may be transported or drawn on a highway, except devices moved by human power or used only on stationary rails or tracks. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 159; RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))

The phenomenon where urban and suburban areas are hotter than surrounding rural areas. A city of one million or more people can average 1.8 to 5.4 degrees F (1 to 3 degrees C) warmer, and on a clear, calm night the difference can reach 22 degrees F (12 degrees C).
The period an asset or component is expected to be available for use, assuming regular and adequate maintenance.
Upward displacement of moving vehicles by raising the road surface, for example with a hump, table or other raised element. A traffic calming technique.

New York City's action plan to improve street safety in every neighborhood and borough, combining expanded enforcement against dangerous moving violations like speeding and failing to yield, new street designs, public outreach, and a legislative agenda to raise penalties for dangerous drivers and give NYC control over its own streets.
The area with a 1% or higher chance of flooding in any given year.

rules.what: Under the NYC Administrative Code, property owners are generally responsible for installing, maintaining and repairing the sidewalk adjacent to their property, including the intersection quadrant for a corner property. For 1, 2 and 3 family homes, the City may make the repairs if the owner fails to and will charge the owner. Owners are not charged for repairs of defects solely related to street trees.
rules.penalty: For 1, 2 and 3 family homes, the City may make repairs the owner fails to make and charge the owner.

rules.what: Parks maintains tree beds for the first two years after planting; after two years, property owners are responsible for tree-bed maintenance.
